title: Koi: Evidence-Guided, Self-Calibrating Planning for Multi-Cloud LLM Inference
content:
Project page
1Tandemn · 2UIUC · 3UC Berkeley · 4NYU · 5ByteDance · 6NVIDIA · *co-first authors
Planning LLM inference across clouds and GPU types means choosing deployments no one has run before. Koi treats every deployment it runs as an experiment that explains why it performed as it did, and uses that answer for every job it plans next.
Results
H100, A100 and RTX PRO 6000 GPUs in three Google Cloud regions; 25 online and batch workloads over ten models. Every planner gets the same snapshots, catalog, checks and language model.
Goodput (tok/s)
Online SLO met (%)
Cost per token (10⁻⁴ $)
Ablation: goodput (tok/s)
1.18× the goodput of the strongest baseline (OpenEvolve) at 20% lower cost per token. Goodput counts only output that meets its SLO. The ablation is a 3-hour simulation: a GPT-5.6 planner with no tools and no memory across ticks gets 71% less goodput than Koi. Koi loses 44% when it stops learning from new runs, and 39% without its causal graph. In 400- and 800-GPU simulations, Koi improves goodput by up to 45% and lowers cost per token by up to 31%.
1 · What Koi does
A fixed rule repeats its mistakes. Koi learns from every job, acts on rising SLO risk, and tries what it is unsure about.
2 · How it works
Why was batch job 2 slow, and what does that mean for a job that has never run?
Typical planner
Koi
3 · Why it is hard
How a job is deployed decides its throughput and cost, for a given workload (here, 2,048-token prompts and 512-token outputs). A planner must choose this for every job at once, mostly for deployments it has never run. (Yes, the A10G is an old GPU, but the same idea holds on newer GPUs too!)
4 · The insight
Search methods keep only the end-to-end score. Koi also measures what limits each deployment.
5 · The mechanism
Each running deployment tests the mechanism that chose it: did the mediator and the outcome both behave as predicted?

report.summary: Koi is a self-calibrating planner that treats each LLM inference deployment as an experiment, using causal evidence about what limits it to plan better multi-cloud GPU jobs.
report.background: Serving LLMs at scale now means renting GPUs across several clouds and generations — H100s here, leftover A100s and RTX PRO 6000s there — while juggling latency SLOs for online traffic and cost per token for batch work. The planner's job is to pick, for every arriving job, which GPU type, region and parallelism to use. The catch: most of those combinations have never been run, so throughput and cost must be guessed. Current approaches fall into two camps — fixed heuristics and autoscalers that repeat the same mistakes, or black-box search (including LLM-driven optimizers such as OpenEvolve) that keeps only an end-to-end score and learns nothing about why a deployment was slow. That makes transfer to unseen hardware poor and expensive, because each wrong guess is paid for in real GPU seconds and missed SLOs.
key_points: Koi's core idea is to measure the mediator, not just the score. Besides end-to-end goodput, it records what actually capped each deployment — memory bandwidth, KV-cache pressure, batching limits — so a result becomes an explanation rather than a single number.

Those explanations are stored in a causal graph that transfers to jobs never run before. When a new workload arrives, Koi asks which bottlenecks the graph says matter and picks a deployment accordingly, instead of re-searching from scratch.

Every live deployment doubles as a test: Koi checks whether the predicted bottleneck and the observed outcome both matched. Mismatches flag the model as stale and trigger recalibration, so the planner's beliefs stay honest as hardware and workloads drift.

In tests spanning H100, A100 and RTX PRO 6000 GPUs across three Google Cloud regions, 25 workloads and ten models, Koi reached 1.18× the goodput of OpenEvolve, the strongest baseline, at 20% lower cost per token.

Ablations show the learning is what matters: a GPT-5.6 planner with no tools or memory scored 71% lower goodput; removing learning from new runs cost 44%, and removing the causal graph cost 39%. At 400–800 GPUs, gains reached 45% goodput and 31% lower cost.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Koi argues that fleet-level efficiency is now a learning problem, not a configuration problem — the same shift autoscaling went through a decade ago. Providers and inference startups running mixed, multi-cloud capacity could squeeze materially more revenue-bearing tokens from hardware they already rent, which matters as GPU supply stays tight and margins thin. For developers, the practical takeaway is to instrument the middle of the stack: capture bottleneck signals like memory-bandwidth utilization and KV-cache occupancy, not just latency, so automated planners can reason about unseen deployments. For regular users, better planners mean faster responses at lower prices, and more reliable SLOs during traffic spikes — the savings from a 20–30% cost-per-token cut tend to show up as cheaper API tiers and more generous rate limits rather than dramatic product changes.
report.tools: To follow up, read the paper (arXiv:2610.24355) and the project page. OpenEvolve, the strongest baseline, is open source and useful for understanding black-box LLM-driven search. For the serving layer, watch vLLM and SGLang (throughput knobs Koi reasons about), llm-d and Ray Serve for fleet orchestration, and SkyPilot for multi-cloud GPU placement. For the bottleneck evidence Koi relies on, Nsight Systems, DCGM metrics and roofline analysis are the practical instrumentation to learn.
